newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG SLALOM WIN EXTENDS WORLD CUP LEAD.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG SLALOM WIN EXTENDS WORLD CUP LEAD.

text.p: Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg kept her Scandinavian cool in demanding conditions on Saturday to win a women's slalom and increase her lead in the overall Alpine skiing World Cup standings.
The 26-year-old now has 718 overall points -- 155 more than Germany's defending title-holder Katja Seizinger, who impressed rivals with ninth place in her first slalom of the winter.
But while Seizinger still favours the speed disciplines, Wiberg has developed into an all-round skier capable of winning in downhill and slalom.
This season, Wiberg has claimed the super-giant slalom in Lake Louise, Canada, and the first of back-to-back slaloms in Semmering, Austria, last week, for a total of 16 career World Cup victories.
She was also second in a super-G in Vail, Colorado, and at the season's opening slaloms at Park City, Utah, and Crans Montana, as well as finishing third in a downhill at Lake Louise.

On Saturday, Wiberg underlined her position as one of the leading figures in slalom this season. Fastest in the first run, she was unruffled by deteriorating conditions and falling snow on the Radvanje piste.

The defending slalom world champion clocked fastest times in both runs for a best aggregate time of one minute 44.55 seconds, on a hill which claimed many prominent victims including Austrian-born Claudia Riegler, who races for New Zealand and has won two slaloms this winter.
"I was worried when I heard we would be racing the second run in reversed 30 order," said Wiberg.
"It made me nervous because I really thought conditions would get worse after every racer and that I wouldn't have a chance. But everything went fine in the end, so I am relieved."
But Wiberg said she would not yet dare dream about the coveted overall title.
"It is far too early to start talking about the overall," said the Swede from Norkopping who lives in Monaco.
"I take each race at a time. I will start thinking about the overall after the world championships (in February in Sestriere)."
Wiberg did, however, say she desperately wanted to win the slalom World Cup title and would therefore begin concentrating more on slalom training.
The Swedish triple world and twice Olympic champion, currently leads the slalom standings on 410 points, ahead of Riegler (289) and Hrovat (237).
Wiberg was also happy to have won her first victory on a slope which almost ended her career in 1993 and forced her to give the Morioka world championships a miss.
"A few years ago I tore my achilles tendon here. Last season I was second and now I win," she said. "It proves that things can always get better."
Local heroine Urska Hrovat recorded her best result of the winter by taking second place on Saturday in 1:45.32.
Despite failing to repeat her victory at Maribor from 1994, she delighted home crowds in the finish area and rolled in the snow in triumph.

"This podium finish was what I needed. Now I feel confident again and know what I have to do to win," said Hrovat. "If Riegler managed to beat Wiberg twice this season then I know I am capable of doing the same."
Italy's Lara Magoni improved from a first run seventh to overall third with 1:46.46 -- her best World Cup performance.
